details:
Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to interconnected hazards that can affect cardiovascular health, bone and muscle strength, immune function, sleep, and psychological well-being. Microgravity, radiation, isolation, and confined environments can lead to gradual physiological and behavioral changes. With limited access to immediate medical support, astronauts must increasingly monitor their own health, recognize changes, and make informed decisions throughout the mission.

To address these challenges, we propose an integrated, onboard-first Astronaut Health Monitoring System that consolidates data from wearable devices, medical equipment, environmental sensors, and astronaut self-reports. The system follows three core principles: Monitor, Understand, and Act. It collects available health indicators, compares measurements against each astronaut's personal baseline, and translates complex data into understandable visualizations and personalized insights. Through an interactive 3D human anatomy, health metrics, historical trends, and color-coded indicators, astronauts can explore different body systems and better understand changes in their health. A personalized action system further encourages daily health activities, exercise routines, recovery, and self-assessments.

A key feature of the proposed system is its onboard-first architecture. Communication delays or temporary disconnections during deep-space missions may limit access to Earth-based medical support. Therefore, local health monitoring, historical data access, and anomaly alerts are designed to remain available onboard. Relevant health records can be prioritized and synchronized with Earth-based medical teams when communication becomes available. This approach aims to support continuous health awareness, earlier recognition of potential changes, and more informed health decisions throughout long-duration missions.

The project combines a digital health monitoring application with a proposed Smart Sleep Mask concept for overnight monitoring. The mask is designed to support the collection of sleep-related and physiological signals, such as sleep patterns and pulse-rate indicators, using appropriate sensors. The digital interface and visualizations were developed with Google Stitch AI, with an emphasis on interactive health data presentation, 3D anatomical exploration, and personalized health insights. The current prototype focuses on the software experience and conceptual system architecture; live sensor integration, hardware implementation, and onboard data analysis remain proposed capabilities. Demonstration data is simulated.

The project's creative approach lies in connecting fragmented health information into a unified, astronaut-centered experience. Rather than presenting isolated measurements, it connects different physiological systems, personal health history, and daily actions. Interactive 3D anatomy makes complex health information easier to explore, while personal baseline comparisons help astronauts understand changes relative to their own health history. The design also considers usability, data reliability, individual differences, microgravity-related health risks, and communication constraints. By connecting monitoring with understandable insights and practical actions, the project explores a more accessible and continuous approach to astronaut health management, with the broader goal of supporting the well-being of crews on future long-duration space missions.
